2. I don’t really accept ChatGPT and other LLM algorithms as AGI. They are purely language oriented, and language is only useful as a tool for representing the real world. A “mind” which cannot associate words with the realities they are intended to represent is just a narrow AI faking general intelligence by playing language games with its audience.

comments.text:
I understand distillation at least coarsely as information compression...the synthetic data is much more refined and focused than the general pool of training knowledge and also incorporates RLHF and other correctness checks allowing a much more condensed and cheaper to run distilled model to be produced. However, try compressing an already compressed file and you see how the improvement goes sigmoidal and your improvement gets exhausted. The potential difference in this case is the distilled model may be able to derive more insight to objective reality than just optimizing the workings of the training model. That isn't clear to me yet. 

The potential downside is akin to Gödel incompleteness in that the distillation papers over too many interesting exceptions that appear in the training set but don't get compiled into the optimized model well. The Titans design pays more attention to these exceptions and may be critical to getting past this oversimplification. But it also has a risk of paying too much attention to false surprises, and we get into a situation where truth testing becomes limiting, and it becomes hazardous to let the AI determine for itself what is true and isn't.

Similarly, AI operates on algorithms and data. It can process information at incredible speeds and find patterns we might miss. But it lacks the core element that drives human intelligence:  agency.

Not to be Buzz Killington or anything, but I just want everyone to know that it's never going to happen. The critical component that AI entirely lacks is sapience, which essentially means that it is incapable of original thought. Because of this, the "intelligence" of AI/AGI will always be constrained by human intelligence. It can be faster, but it cannot be more intelligent. 

To really understand these ideas, it's important to consider that the human mind is vastly more powerful than most people give it credit for. Sure, AI can process vast amounts of information extremely quickly, but it is also extremely limited in ways that make an ant look like a genius in comparison. A living mind has the ability to continuously adapt and consider an essentially infinite number of potential solutions to any problem at any moment. This is what I'd call logical resolution, but that's already taken, so let's call it intellectual resolution. The intellectual resolution of an AI is extremely low, which means that it is extremely limited when it comes to problem solving. Each successive generation of AI increases its intellectual resolution, but this also demands exponentially more storage space and processing power. Eventually — like many years in the future — it's possible that AI will be able to closely mimic humans in nearly every way, but, I'm sorry to say, this idea of a singularity is 100% hype.
